name: Kwale
confidence_why: Dutton 1970, a survey sketch that says its own sketches still need checking against fuller material, calls Kwale stress phonemic on the strength of ma'da 'sun' beside 'maya 'mountain', while Kikkawa 1999, a one-line draft SIL phonology sheet, says only that stress is predictable, and neither work states where stress falls, so no rule can be given.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dutton gives no positional rule: Kwale (Uare) is not tonal, and primary stress is treated as phonemic (contrastive), shown by the near-minimal pair ma'da 'sun' (final) vs 'maya 'mountain' (initial/penultimate). The only regularity stated is that in sequences of identical vowels the second vowel carries the stress unless a glottal stop separates them. His stress-marked wordlist shows penultimate stress as the commonest placement, with final and antepenultimate forms.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (only primary stress is marked).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; the claim is that stress is contrastive, illustrated by ma'da 'sun' vs 'maya 'mountain'. The wordlist shows penultimate stress as the majority pattern with final (i'si 'belly', nu'ne 'breast') and antepenultimate ('ikuɣa 'bird', 'kuruɣa 'blind', u'buae 'boy') forms. Same-vowel sequences are stressed on the second vowel unless broken by a glottal stop.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: isolated citation forms in a survey wordlist ('basic' vocabulary, Appendix 3.9). Primary stress marked on every Kwale form; the author states the sketches 'are based on survey materials and need to be checked against more extensive material' (p. 916).
new_statements.identity_note: Dutton 1970 calls the language 'Kwale' (Glottolog Uare, uare1241; ISO ksj) and says it has two dialects, Garia (around Geresi) = Glottolog Garihe (gari1255) and Kwale (around Kwale village) = Nuclear Uare (nucl1626); the stress statement is for the Kwale variety collected in Kwale village (wordlist column 'KWALE KWALE'). The p. 916 sentence covers the Kwalean and Manubaran languages jointly; the p. 917 sentence is in the Kwale phoneme sketch. Dutton also says Kwale and Humene (hume1246) have nearly identical phonologies.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Kwale has an empty rule; the only existing statement (Dutton 1970: 916-917) says 'stress seems to be phonemic in each [Kwalean/Manubaran language]' and, for Kwale, 'Stress is phonemic, e.g., ma'da sun and 'maya mountain.' Kikkawa 1999 says the opposite about the type: stress is predictable, i.e. non-contrastive. Neither source gives a placement rule, so the contradiction is on contrastiveness, not on position. Kikkawa is the later, dedicated SIL phonology sketch (data checked 1992, revised 1999) but is a one-line draft statement with no evidence shown.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The whole suprasegmental section is the one sentence 'Stress is predictable.' The source asserts that stress is non-contrastive (rule-governed) but gives no rule, no position, and no example with stress marked; the apostrophes in the syllable-pattern examples ('a.'o 'prawn', 'u.e.'o.he 'bend') are the orthographic glottal stop < ' >, per the Conventions section, not stress marks. No tone or length statement either. Placement therefore cannot be read from this work.
new_statements.identity_note: Kikkawa 1999 names the language 'Uare (Kware, Kwale)' with 'Kware' as the major village and data checked 1992/1999 by an SIL linguist; Dutton's 1967 recording (and the 1970 sketch built on it) is from Kuale Village in the Rigo area. Both are the same Kwalean language (ISO ksj, Glottolog uare1241); no dialect split is stated in either source. Works 0 and 1 in the target list are one and the same document (SIL archive item 42300).

readall_conflicts: The two written sources disagree on whether Kwale/Uare word stress is contrastive. Dutton 1970 (Pacific Linguistics C-13, Appendix 3.7, p. 916 and p. 917, already in the catalog) says 'None of the languages is tonal but stress seems to be phonemic in each' and, for Kwale, 'Stress is phonemic, e.g., ma'da sun and 'maya mountain' (final vs initial stress in two disyllables that are not a true minimal pair). Kikkawa 1999 (SIL Organised Phonology Data, p. 4) says only 'Stress is predictable.' Neither source states where stress falls, and Kikkawa's OPD marks stress on no example (its apostrophes are glottal stops), so the disagreement is on type (phonemic vs predictable) and no placement rule can be extracted from either. The PARADISEC audio item says nothing.
